lead: A continuous-time system is linear time-invariant (LTI) when it obeys two rules. Linearity: scaling and adding inputs scales and adds the outputs in the same way. Time invariance: an input delayed by t₀ seconds gives the same output, delayed by t₀ seconds. Together the two rules mean the system is fixed by one signal, its impulse response, so one convolution integral gives the output for every input. Audio equalisers, RC and RLC filters, amplifiers working in their linear range and transmission lines are all modelled as LTI systems.
prereq: You need: the classification of systems (linearity, time invariance, causality, stability) and the unit impulse δ(t) and unit step u(t).

blocks.text: Write a continuous-time system as an operator T: the input x(t) goes in and the output y(t)=T{x(t)} comes out, with t in seconds. The system is linear if, for every pair of inputs and every pair of constants,
T{a x₁(t) + b x₂(t)} = a T{x₁(t)} + b T{x₂(t)}
blocks.where: x₁(t) and x₂(t) are any two inputs, a and b are any constants, and y₁=T{x₁}, y₂=T{x₂} are their outputs. The rule packs two properties: additivity (a=b=1) and homogeneity or scaling (b=0). Together they are called the superposition principle.

blocks.text: Put a=b=0 and the rule says T{0}=0: a linear system gives zero output for zero input. This zero-in, zero-out check is quick but only necessary; y(t)=x²(t) passes it and is still nonlinear.
if x(t) → y(t), then x(t − t₀) → y(t − t₀)
blocks.where: t₀ is any delay in seconds (positive t₀ delays, negative t₀ advances). The rule says the system's behaviour does not depend on clock time. Some syllabi call this shift invariance.

blocks.text: A system that obeys both rules is LTI. Being LTI says nothing about causality or stability; those are separate tests, done on the impulse response in causality and BIBO stability of LTI systems.

sections.h3: Testing a formula: two paths that must meet

blocks.text: Each test compares two paths through the system. If the two paths give different outputs for even one choice of inputs, the property fails.

items: Linearity, path 1: combine first. Form a x₁ + b x₂, pass it through T.
Linearity, path 2: pass x₁ and x₂ through T separately, then form a y₁ + b y₂.
Compare. A mismatch for one choice of inputs proves the system nonlinear. A match for one choice proves nothing; to prove linearity, do the comparison with symbols for all inputs.
Time invariance, path 1: delay the input to x(t − t₀), pass it through T. Write the result as y<sub>d</sub>(t), the output for the delayed input.
Time invariance, path 2: take the original output y(t) and replace every t by t − t₀.
Compare y<sub>d</sub>(t) with y(t − t₀). Equal for every t and t₀ means time-invariant.

blocks.text: Three patterns settle most exam systems. An added constant, y(t)=3x(t)+2, breaks linearity because T{0}=2, but it keeps time invariance. A multiplier that depends on t, y(t)=t·x(t), keeps linearity but breaks time invariance. Scaling the time axis, y(t)=x(2t), is linear but time-varying: with x(t)=t and t₀=1 s, the delayed input x(t−1)=t−1 gives y<sub>d</sub>(t)=2t−1, while y(t−1)=2(t−1)=2t−2. At t=1 s these are 1 and 0. The delay is squeezed along with the signal, so the two paths do not meet.

sections.h3: Why LTI is worth the trouble

blocks.text: Any input can be written as a continuous sum, that is an integral, of shifted impulses: x(t)=∫ x(τ)δ(t−τ)dτ, taken over all τ. This is the sifting property of δ(t); τ is a dummy variable that runs along the input's time axis. If the system's response to δ(t) is h(t), time invariance gives the response h(t−τ) to δ(t−τ), and linearity lets you weight each response by x(τ) and add them all. The result is the convolution integral of convolution integral and its evaluation.

So one measured signal, h(t), predicts the response to every input. The same fact gives the frequency response H(jω) and the transfer function H(s), treated in Fourier analysis and Laplace transform analysis. Squarers, limiters, rectifiers and time-scalers are not LTI and need other methods. Most real circuits are LTI only over a range: an op-amp stage is linear until its output saturates.

examples.question: Test the system y(t)=3x(t)+2 for linearity and time invariance. For linearity use x₁(t)=1, x₂(t)=2, a=2 and b=3. For time invariance use x(t)=t and a delay t₀=2 s, and evaluate both paths at t=5 s. State whether the system is LTI.
steps: Path 1 (combine first): a x₁ + b x₂ = 2(1)+3(2)=8. Then T{8}=3(8)+2=26.
Path 2 (separately): T{x₁}=3(1)+2=5 and T{x₂}=3(2)+2=8. Then a y₁ + b y₂ = 2(5)+3(8)=10+24=34.
26 ≠ 34, so the system is not linear. One counterexample is enough. (Also T{0}=2 ≠ 0.)
Time invariance, path 1: the delayed input is x(t−2)=t−2, so y<sub>d</sub>(t)=3(t−2)+2=3t−4.
Path 2: the original output is y(t)=3t+2; replace t by t−2: y(t−2)=3(t−2)+2=3t−4.

The two expressions are the same for every t; at t=5 s both give 3(5)−4=11. Because the rule 3x+2 has no t of its own, the same algebra works for any input and any delay, so the system is time-invariant.
Linear fails, time invariance holds: the system is not LTI.
examples.answer: Not linear (26 ≠ 34) but time-invariant (both paths give 11 at t=5 s), so y(t)=3x(t)+2 is not an LTI system.

examples.question: Test y(t)=t·x(t) for linearity and time invariance. For the time test use x(t)=u(t), t₀=1 s and evaluate at t=2 s.
steps: Linearity with symbols: T{a x₁ + b x₂}=t[a x₁(t)+b x₂(t)]=a·t x₁(t)+b·t x₂(t)=a y₁ + b y₂. This holds for every input and constant, so the system is linear.
Delayed input: x(t−1)=u(t−1). The system multiplies whatever arrives by the present time t, so y<sub>d</sub>(t)=t·u(t−1). At t=2 s: y<sub>d</sub>(2)=2×1=2.
Shifted output: y(t)=t·u(t), so y(t−1)=(t−1)·u(t−1). At t=2 s: y(2−1)=1×1=1.
2 ≠ 1, so the system is time-varying. The multiplier t is a clock inside the system.
examples.answer: Linear but time-varying (2 ≠ 1 at t=2 s), so not LTI.

traps: Using t₀ for the delay and then replacing t by t − t₀ inside the system's own multiplier: for y(t)=t·x(t), only the input is delayed in path 1, so y<sub>d</sub>(t)=t·x(t−t₀), not (t−t₀)x(t−t₀).
Calling y(t)=x(2t) time-invariant because the rule has no t outside the input: the factor 2 scales the time axis itself, and the delay test fails (1 ≠ 0 at t=1 s with x(t)=t and t₀=1 s).
An added constant breaks linearity, not time invariance: y(t)=3x(t)+2 is time-invariant but not LTI. Some students call it "linear" because its graph against x is a straight line.
Proving linearity with one numerical pair: a match for one pair proves nothing. Use symbols, or one mismatch to disprove.
Time-invariant does not mean the output is constant in time. It means the rule that turns input into output does not change with time.

quiz.q: Define an LTI system in one sentence.
quiz.a: A system that obeys superposition (T{a x₁ + b x₂}=a y₁ + b y₂) and in which an input delayed by t₀ gives the output delayed by t₀.

quiz.q: Name the two properties that together make up superposition.
quiz.a: Additivity, T{x₁+x₂}=y₁+y₂, and homogeneity (scaling), T{a x}=a y.

quiz.q: Why must a linear system satisfy T{0}=0, and why is this check not enough to prove linearity?
quiz.a: Put a=b=0 in the superposition rule: the left side is T{0} and the right side is 0. It is not enough because nonlinear systems such as y=x² also give zero output for zero input.

quiz.q: Test y(t)=x(t)+3 for linearity using x₁=1, x₂=2, a=b=1.
quiz.a: Path 1: T{1+2}=T{3}=3+3=6. Path 2: T{1}+T{2}=4+5=9. Since 6 ≠ 9, the system is not linear.

quiz.q: For y(t)=x(2t), use x(t)=t, t₀=1 s and t=1 s to show the system is time-varying.
quiz.a: Delayed input x(t−1)=t−1 gives y<sub>d</sub>(t)=2t−1, so y<sub>d</sub>(1)=1. Shifted output y(t−1)=2(t−1)=2t−2; at t=1 s this is 0. Since 1 ≠ 0 the system is time-varying.

quiz.q: Is y(t)=2x(t)+1 linear? Is it time-invariant? Is it LTI? Give one line of working for each.
quiz.a: Not linear: T{0}=1 ≠ 0. Time-invariant: the delayed input gives 2x(t−t₀)+1, which equals y(t−t₀). Not LTI, because both properties are needed.

quiz.q: A system is linear and time-invariant. Its response to δ(t) is h(t). Explain in two sentences why its response to δ(t−3) is h(t−3) and its response to 5δ(t) is 5h(t).
quiz.a: Time invariance: delaying the input by 3 s delays the output by 3 s, so δ(t−3) gives h(t−3). Homogeneity: scaling the input by 5 scales the output by 5, so 5δ(t) gives 5h(t).

beyond: Not for the exam. Real devices are LTI only in a range, so engineers measure how far they stray: total harmonic distortion (THD) in audio amplifiers and intermodulation tests in radio receivers both measure the departure from linearity. When the departure is large, models such as Hammerstein and Wiener models (a static nonlinearity joined to an LTI block) or linear parameter-varying (LPV) models take over. Search for "total harmonic distortion measurement" and "Hammerstein model" to see how this is done in industry.
